title: Vaccination and Sterilization
content:
Vaccination and timely spaying/neutering are your main defense against fatal diseases and behavioral problems.

## When to Start Vaccinating Puppies and Adult Dogs
Vaccination is mandatory, even if the dog does not interact with other animals. Some viruses can be brought home on clothing or shoes.

*Puppy Schedule (Basic Protocol):*
*First vaccine* (distemper, parvovirus enteritis, adenovirus, parainfluenza). - 6–8 weeks
*Mandatory deworming* 10–14 days before vaccination.
*Second vaccine* (booster for first components). - 10–12 weeks
*Rabies is added in some regions.*
*Rabies Vaccination* (if not done earlier). - 12–16 weeks
! Annual revaccination for all components.

*Important:* During the period between the first and last vaccinations (quarantine), it is forbidden to walk the puppy outside and allow it to contact unvaccinated dogs.

*Adult Dog:*
Adult dogs are revaccinated annually against major viral diseases and rabies. Do not miss this deadline!

## Optimal Age for Spaying/Neutering
The timing depends on the dog's size and gender.
*Small breeds (up to 10 kg)* - 5–6 months 
*Risk of hormone-dependent problems is minimal, they recover quickly.
*Medium breeds (10–25 kg)* - 6–9 months
*Standard age before the first heat cycle in females.
*Large and Giant breeds (from 25 kg)* - 12 to 18 months
*It is recommended to wait until growth plates are fully closed and joints are mature (to prevent orthopedic problems).

*Pros and Cons of Early Spaying/Neutering (before 6 months):*
*PRO:* Reduces aggression, eliminates unwanted pregnancies, almost completely excludes mammary cancer in females.
*CON (especially for large breeds):* Some studies link very early sterilization to an increased risk of orthopedic problems (dysplasia) and, in rare cases, certain types of cancer in large dogs.

**Conclusion:** Do not fear spaying/neutering — it extends life and improves behavior quality. For small and medium breeds, the operation can be performed before one year. For large breeds, wait for full physical maturity after consulting with a veterinarian.

title: Emergency Aid: Poisoning
content:
A dog owner must know how to act in an emergency. Quick response can save a pet's life.

## Critical Poisoning: Immediate Action
If you suspect your dog has swallowed poison, call your veterinarian or an emergency clinic immediately!

*Toxin: Rat poison (rodenticides). Source: Baits in basements, outside.*
*Action: URGENT!* Induce vomiting (only if the doctor allows and no more than 1–2 hours have passed). Immediately take the dog to the veterinarian for an antidote (Vitamin K). Do not wait for symptoms!

*Toxin: Antifreeze (ethylene glycol). Source: Car leak.*
*Action:* Deadly even in small doses. Symptoms (staggering gait, vomiting) quickly disappear, but the kidneys are dying. Time is counted in hours.

*Toxin: Chocolate. Source: Sweets.*
*Action:* Toxic due to theobromine. The darker the chocolate, the more dangerous. Immediately consult a doctor, especially if a large dose was consumed.

*Toxin: Xylitol. Source: Gum, toothpaste, diet products.*
*Action: URGENT!* Causes a sharp drop in blood sugar (hypoglycemia) and liver failure.

*Remember:* Do not induce vomiting if the dog is unconscious, having difficulty breathing, or has swallowed a corrosive substance (e.g., household chemicals). Always follow the veterinarian's instructions.

title: Emergency Aid: Heatstroke
content:
A dog owner must know how to act in an emergency. Quick response can save a pet's life.

## First Aid for Heatstroke
Dogs cool down only through breathing (heavy panting) and their paws, so they overheat easily, especially in summer and during intense activity.

*Critical Signs:*
*Excessive, noisy panting* (gasping).
*Gums are bright red* or, conversely, very pale.
*Tremors, vomiting, disorientation.*

*Immediate Aid (Urgent):*
*Move* the dog to a cool place or shade.
*Cool:* Wet the coat with cool (not icy!) water. Pay special attention to the neck, armpits, and groin area, where major blood vessels run.
*Do not use ice* — this can cause shock or constrict blood vessels, worsening cooling.
*Urgently take* the dog to the clinic to monitor temperature and prevent organ damage.

title: Emergency Aid: Tick Bite
content:
A dog owner must know how to act in an emergency. Quick response can save a pet's life.

## Tick Bite and Piroplasmosis Symptoms
Ticks transmit Piroplasmosis (Babesiosis) — a disease that destroys red blood cells and is deadly.

*Your Actions:*
*Tick removal:* Use a special tick remover hook or tweezers. Twist the tick out, do not pull.

*Piroplasmosis (Babesiosis) Symptoms:* Monitor the dog for 3–7 days after the bite.
*Lethargy, apathy, refusal to eat.*
*Fever.*
*Change in urine color* (from dark yellow to brown or even red).

*Urgent Vet Visit:* If you notice these symptoms, do not wait! Piroplasmosis develops rapidly and requires immediate treatment.

**Conclusion:** Always use regular tick protection (tablets, drops) and immediately react to critical symptoms. Delay in case of poisoning or Piroplasmosis can cost a life.

title: Feeding: What is Strictly Forbidden
content:
## What You Absolutely Cannot Feed Dogs
These foods can cause severe poisoning, internal organ damage, or death.

*Product: Chocolate*
*Danger and Consequences:* Contains theobromine, a toxin that accumulates in the body. Causes vomiting, diarrhea, tremors, and damage to the heart/nervous system.

*Product: Xylitol (sugar substitute)*
*Danger and Consequences:* Found in gum, toothpaste, diet products. Causes a sharp drop in blood sugar and acute liver failure.

*Product: Grapes and Raisins*
*Danger and Consequences:* The exact mechanism of toxicity is unknown, but even a small amount can cause kidney failure in sensitive dogs.

*Product: Onions and Garlic*
*Danger and Consequences:* Contain compounds that destroy red blood cells and cause anemia.

*Product: Alcohol*
*Danger and Consequences:* Even small doses can cause poisoning, coma, and death.

*Product: Tubular bones (chicken, rabbit)*
*Danger and Consequences: Critically dangerous!* Bones splinter into sharp shards that can puncture the stomach or intestines.

*Product: Avocado*
*Danger and Consequences:* Contains the toxin persin, which is dangerous to the heart in large quantities and can cause digestive upset.

*Product: Macadamia Nuts*
*Danger and Consequences:* Toxin causes lethargy, vomiting, tremors, and temporary hind limb paralysis.

*Important Note:* Avoid feeding raw meat of unknown origin (risk of parasites) and milk (often causes diarrhea).

title: Feeding: How to Choose a Diet
content:
Proper feeding is the best prevention of diseases. A dog, unlike a cat, is not a strict carnivore, but still requires a balanced protein diet.

## Choosing Food by Age, Breed, and Activity
Choose food where an animal protein source (chicken, turkey, lamb, fish) is listed first, not cereals or by-products.

*Parameters: Age*
*Selection Features:*
1. *Puppies:* High protein, fat, and calcium content for bone growth. 
2. *Adult:* Balanced diet for weight and energy maintenance. 
3. *Senior:* Fewer calories, often more fiber and joint supplements (glucosamine, chondroitin).

*Parameters: Breed/Size*
*Selection Features:*
1. *Small:* Small kibble, increased calorie density (fast metabolism). 
2. *Large:* Carefully balanced calcium and phosphorus content to avoid excessively rapid growth and joint problems.

*Parameters: Activity*
*Selection Features:*
1. *High (Working, sporting):* Food with increased fat and protein content for energy. 
2. *Low (House dogs):* Food with controlled calories (Light/Sterilized) to prevent obesity.

*Parameters: Health Problems*
*Selection Features:*
In case of allergies, kidney diseases, or digestive issues, a veterinary diet is used (only as prescribed by a doctor).

**Conclusion:** Avoid economy-class foods. Choose *Super Premium* or *Holistic* with a clear indication of meat ingredients at the beginning of the list. Never give the dog "treats" from your table — this leads to begging, imbalance, and digestive problems.

title: Equipment: How to Choose a Collar, Harness, and Muzzle
content:
Properly selected equipment is a matter of safety, comfort, and training. The wrong choice can harm health and spoil the walk.

## How to Choose a Leash and Collar/Harness
The choice between a collar and a harness depends on the breed, size, and behavioral characteristics of the dog.

*Collar*
*Advantages:* Allows better control of the dog. Ideal for training basic commands. Easy to put on and take off.
*Features:* Suitable for most medium and large breeds with a healthy neck. *Important:* Do not use on dogs that constantly pull the leash (risk of neck/trachea injury).

*Harness (Classic Y-shaped)*
*Advantages:* Relieves strain on the neck and distributes it across the chest and shoulders. Ideal for small breeds (trachea protection), brachycephalic dogs (Pugs, Bulldogs), and dogs with neck/back issues.
*Features:* Ideal for dogs that pull strongly (for comfort, but not for correction). Ensure the harness does not chafe the armpits.

*Harness (Correctional, with front clip)*
*Advantages:* Helps discourage pulling, as the pull redirects the dog sideways.
*Features:* Suitable for dogs that need behavioral correction without causing pain.

*Important Tip:* Do not use retractable leashes for puppies and poorly trained dogs. Retractable leashes can encourage pulling, and a sudden jerk during locking can injure the dog.

title: Is a Muzzle Necessary and How to Choose One
content:
A muzzle is a safety tool, not a punishment. In many public places, wearing a muzzle is mandatory by law.

## When a Muzzle is Needed:
*Public transport, veterinary clinics.*
*If the dog is prone to picking up trash* or poisons outside.
*For safety* (if the dog shows aggression towards people or other animals).

## How to Choose the Right Muzzle (Critically Important!):
*Type:* Choose a *basket muzzle* (leather or plastic). It must allow the dog to open its mouth and stick out its tongue for cooling (panting), otherwise the dog may suffer heatstroke in hot weather.
*Form:* *Tube muzzles (closed)* or *loop muzzles* are used only for short-term manipulations at the vet, not for regular walks.

**Conclusion:** Choose equipment according to its purpose: collar for training, harness for comfort and neck protection. The muzzle must be safe and allow the dog to breathe.

title: Training: Commands for Safety
content:
Training is not just tricks; it is a language of communication with the dog and a guarantee of its safety outside. You should start at the earliest stages of the puppy's life.

## How to Stop Your Dog from Picking Things up Outside (The "Leave It" Command)
The "Leave It" command is one of the most vital, as it prevents poisoning.

*Create an association:* First, practice the command at home. Place a low-value treat (or toy) on the floor. When the dog reaches for it, firmly say "Leave it!" or "No!"

*Redirection:* At the moment of distraction, immediately offer a much tastier treat from your hand. The dog should understand: refusing something bad brings a reward from the owner.

*Practicing outside:* Start in places where there are no strong distractions. If the dog sees trash but hasn't taken it yet, use the command "Heel!" or "Come!" and pass the dangerous spot. If it takes it — use "Leave It!" and immediately offer to trade for a treat it really likes.

*Never hit or yell* at the dog when it has already taken something. Otherwise, it will just learn to swallow the prize quickly so you don't have time to take it away.

**Conclusion:** Training should be consistent and positive. The dog should want to cooperate with you because it is rewarding and pleasant. The "Leave It" command is practiced not for punishment, but for exchanging a dangerous find for something better.

title: Training: House Training
content:
## How to House Train (Indoors/Outdoors)
The secret to success is regularity and positive reinforcement.

*Puppies (Training to use a pad or go outside):*
*Schedule:* Puppies need to go to the toilet immediately after waking up, after eating, and after playing. These are your "golden" moments for walks.
*Praise:* When the puppy goes outside (or on the pad) — praise it enthusiastically, give a treat, and play.
*Accidents inside:* If the puppy has an accident indoors, *NEVER rub its nose in it or punish it.* It will not understand why it is being scolded. Simply clean the area quietly, using products that eliminate the odor so that it does not return there by smell.

*Adult Dogs:*
If an adult dog suddenly starts eliminating indoors, first rule out illness (cystitis, kidney failure). If the dog is healthy, it may be due to stress, separation anxiety, or inadequate walks.

title: Frequent Disputes: Feeding from the Table
content:
Owners often fall into two camps regarding discipline and treats. Here is the advice from cynologists and veterinarians.

## Should You Feed Your Dog from the Table: Opinion of Veterinarians and Cynologists
*Answer: Absolutely not.*

*Opinion: "It's a sign of love"*
*Argument:* The owner wants to share what they are eating and sees the pet's pleasure.
*Critical Note:* Our food is not balanced for a dog (too much salt, spices, sugar, fat). This leads to obesity, pancreatitis, gastritis, and dietary imbalance.

*Opinion: Behavioral Aspect*
*Argument: "Just one bite won't hurt".*
*Critical Note:* Any bite is reinforcement for begging. The dog quickly learns that pestering the owner brings a reward. This ruins its behavior at the table and when guests are eating.

*Opinion: Risk of Poisoning*
*Argument: "It's just meat/bread"*
*Critical Note:* There is a high risk of giving the dog a forbidden product (e.g., onion or garlic in a dish, or a bone that will splinter).

**Conclusion:** Your love should be expressed through high-quality food, games, and training. If you want to give a treat, use special dog treats or pieces of safe foods (e.g., carrots), but only away from your table and as a reward for a command.

title: Punishment in Training
content:
## Should You Punish Your Dog: The Debate on Positive vs. Forceful Approach
*Answer: Physical punishment and yelling do not work and harm the relationship.*

Cynologists worldwide are increasingly leaning towards the *positive reinforcement* method.

*Approach: Positive Reinforcement*
*Essence:* We reward (with treats, praise) correct behavior and ignore minor mistakes.
*Consequences for the Dog:* The dog enjoys learning, understands WHAT is expected of it. Trust in the owner is strengthened.

*Approach: Forceful/Punishment (yelling, poking, hitting)*
*Essence:* Physically or morally punishing incorrect behavior.
*Consequences for the Dog:* The dog learns to fear the owner. The behavior doesn't disappear but is masked (it does bad things when you are away). Aggression related to fear may develop.

*Approach: "Punishment" for Mistakes*
*Essence:* If you catch the dog in the act of unwanted behavior (e.g., chewing a shoe), firmly say "Leave it!" and redirect its attention to an allowed toy.

*Important Point:* Punishment is only meaningful if it occurs at the moment the misbehavior is committed. *Punishing a dog 10 minutes later for an accident is pointless.* The dog will not link the two events.

**Conclusion:** Instead of punishment, use redirection and environmental management (put away shoes, block access to trash). Build training on trust, not fear.
